title: unstakeFor permits the migrator to withdraw NFTs of any beneficiary, including users who staked directly via stake()
description:
`unstakeFor(beneficiary, amount)` is gated by `onlyMigrator` and `whenNotPaused` but performs no check that the position it is unstaking was originally deposited via `stakeFor` by the current migrator (or any migrator at all). The `users[beneficiary]` ledger is undifferentiated — it co-mingles positions created by `stake(amount)` (direct staker, msg.sender == beneficiary) and positions created by `stakeFor(beneficiary, amount)` (migrator-deposited). The only precondition is `users[beneficiary].amount >= amount` (line 547). Crucially, line 558 transfers the ERC1155 principal to `msg.sender` — i.e. the migrator — not to the beneficiary. The migrator can therefore enumerate any address with a non-zero stake (via the public `users(address)` getter) and call `unstakeFor(victim, users[victim].amount)` to pull the victim's NFTs into the migrator's own wallet. The pending phUSD is correctly routed to the beneficiary by the refactored `_safePay(beneficiary, pending)` on line 552, but the principal is gone.

Code references:
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:521-541` — `stakeFor` creates positions credited to `users[beneficiary]`.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:458-483` — `stake` also writes to `users[msg.sender]`, indistinguishable in storage from `stakeFor`-created positions.
- `lib/phoenix-nft-staking/src/NFTStakerV2.sol:558` — `stakedToken.safeTransferFrom(address(this), msg.sender, stakedId, amount, "")` sends principal to the migrator, not the beneficiary.
impact: All NFT principal held in the staker is at the discretion of a single migrator address. In the documented migration scenario (~139 id-4 NFTs converted to id-6 and staked via the helper), a migrator that goes off-design or is repurposed can drain every NFT — both those it migrated in and those that pre-existed via direct `stake()` calls — without invoking any other privileged role (pauser, owner) and without needing the contract paused. Unlike `withdrawRewardToken`, there is no `paused()` precondition on `unstakeFor`, so the confiscation can be performed at any time while the contract is operating normally. Note: the migrator is owner-set and revocable, so a malicious owner argument falls under the project's accepted centralisation envelope; this finding focuses on the structural code defect that the user's principal ledger and the migrator's withdrawal capability are not separated.
recommendation: Either (a) tag positions at creation with a marker indicating they were deposited via `stakeFor` (e.g. a sibling mapping `migratorDeposited[address] -> uint256`) and constrain `unstakeFor` to only operate on the migrator-deposited subset, or (b) remove `unstakeFor` entirely — it is not in the migration plan and no on-chain use case is documented for it. If (b), users who staked via `stakeFor` retain the standard `unstake(amount)` path which pays principal to themselves.
attack_scenario:
1. Owner deploys NFTStakerV2 and sets migrator = MigrationHelper.
2. Several users discover the new staker contract directly and call `stake(10)` each, with msg.sender == self. Their positions land in `users[self]`.
3. At some later point the owner needs to rotate the migrator (e.g. helper bug fix, new migration phase) and calls `setMigrator(newMigrator)` where newMigrator is a contract that, by design or accident, calls `unstakeFor` on every known staker.
4. newMigrator iterates over discovered staker addresses (events are public) and calls `unstakeFor(victim, users(victim).amount)`. The NFTs land in newMigrator's wallet; the victim's `users[victim].amount` becomes 0; the victim receives a phUSD `Claimed` event for their pending rewards but no NFT return.
5. Victims have no on-chain recourse — their position has been zeroed and the NFTs are out of the staker.
